Đối chiếu paraphrasing: setting a world record record setting feat perilous expedition — chuyến thám hiểm nguy hiểm: Dễ chọn vì cùng câu bằng chứng có “exceptionally perilous expedition” Nhưng đó là sự kiện sau chuyến bay, ứng với chỗ trống 9, không phải thành tựu đạt được nhờ bay 48 giờ. moderate renown — mức độ nổi tiếng vừa phải: Câu trước nói Wegener không phải người vô danh (“hardly an obscure figure”), nhưng chỗ trống 8 hỏi thành tựu cụ thể của chuyến bay.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 35 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: an episode followed by his much-publicised but 9. ___ along the shores of Spitsbergen . Ô 9 cần một cụm danh từ chỉ sự việc diễn ra ở Spitsbergen sau chuyến bay. Từ “but” cho thấy cụm cần điền còn nêu một đặc điểm khác ngoài việc được đưa tin nhiều.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào địa danh đặc biệt Spitsbergen => ta tìm đến câu (5), đoạn 4. Đoạn 4
explanation.step3: Đoạn 4: Back in 1906 he and his brother Emil had stayed aloft in a hot-air balloon for 48 hours, setting a world record ; and between 1906 and 1908 he took part in a widely reported and exceptionally perilous expedition to the Spitsbergen coast .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: perilous expedition Câu hoàn chỉnh: an episode followed by his much-publicised but perilous expedition along the shores of Spitsbergen. (sau chuyến bay đó là chuyến thám hiểm được đưa tin nhiều nhưng nguy hiểm của ông dọc bờ biển Spitsbergen.) => Khớp với dự đoán về một sự việc tại Spitsbergen: bài đọc gọi đó là chuyến thám hiểm nguy hiểm (“perilous expedition”). Đối chiếu paraphrasing: much publicised widely reported perilous expedition giữ nguyên along the shores of Spitsbergen to the Spitsbergen coast record-setting feat “ — thành tích lập kỷ lục ”: cùng câu có “setting a world record”, Nhưng chi tiết ấy nói về chuyến bay, không phải sự việc ở Spitsbergen. moderate renown “ — mức độ nổi tiếng vừa phải ”: Có thể liên tưởng đến “much-publicised”, nhưng đây là mức độ nổi tiếng, không phải một sự việc diễn ra dọc bờ biển. scholarly dispute “ — cuộc tranh luận học thuật ”: Đoạn 2 có “centre of a controversy”, nhưng đó là tranh luận về lý thuyết, không phải chuyến đi Spitsbergen.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 36 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: His textbook on the upper atmosphere had, moreover, brought him to the notice of 10. ___ of scientists in Germany . Dự đoán: Cần một cụm danh từ chỉ nhóm người biết đến Wegener nhờ cuốn sách.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc đến ý cuốn sách giáo khoa về tầng khí quyển trên (“textbook on the upper atmosphere”). Đoạn 4 nhắc đến một cuốn sách giáo khoa (“a textbook”) => bắt đầu đọc câu (6). Đoạn 4 — a textbook
explanation.step3: Đoạn 4: Among a small circle of German meteorologists and atmospheric physicists he had additionally made his name as the author of a clutch of notable scientific papers and of a textbook , The Physics of the Upper Air (1911) . Wegener được một nhóm nhỏ các nhà khoa học Đức biết đến với tư cách tác giả cuốn sách.
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: small circle Câu hoàn chỉnh: His textbook on the upper atmosphere had, moreover, brought him to the notice of small circle of scientists in Germany. (Cuốn sách giáo khoa về tầng khí quyển trên đã khiến Wegener được một nhóm nhỏ các nhà khoa học ở Đức biết đến.) => Khớp với dự đoán về nhóm người và cụm chỉ nhóm nhỏ trong bài. Lưu ý: Đề thiếu mạo từ *a* trước chỗ trống, nên câu tiếng Anh sau khi điền chưa đúng ngữ pháp. Đáp án trong danh sách vẫn là small circle ; không tự thêm từ vào đáp án. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: small circle 10. ___ of scientists in Germany made his name brought him to the notice of a textbook + The Physics of the Upper Air His textbook on the upper atmosphere moderate renown “ danh tiếng ở mức vừa phải ”: bài nói Wegener trở nên có tiếng (“made his name”). Nhưng chỗ trống hỏi nhóm người biết đến ông, không hỏi mức độ nổi tiếng. broad field “ lĩnh vực rộng ”: Sai vì đây là phạm vi nghiên cứu, không phải một nhóm nhà khoa học. narrow inquiry “ hướng nghiên cứu hẹp ”: Từ chỉ quy mô nhỏ (“small”) có thể gây nhầm, nhưng inquiry là hoạt động nghiên cứu, không phải nhóm người.

questions.prompt: In the fifth paragraph, what is Adamczyk trying to do?
options: describe what first drew him to write about Wegener
explain why Wegener switched between so many fields
recommend that the book be read in its entirety
point out which parts of Wegener's life he finds most compelling
questions.correct: recommend that the book be read in its entirety

explanation.step1: In the fifth paragraph , what is Adamczyk trying to do ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Adamczyk muốn đạt mục đích gì khi viết đoạn văn thứ năm?
explanation.step2: Đếm các đoạn văn xuôi từ đoạn 2, vì đoạn 1 chỉ ghi “Introduction”. Vậy đoạn văn thứ năm là đoạn 6 trong nguồn. Ta bắt đầu đọc từ câu mở đầu bằng “Anyone who follows”. Đoạn 6 — Anyone who follows
explanation.step3: Đoạn 6: Anyone who follows the particulars of his career closely will notice that Wegener repeatedly set aside a given line of enquiry — occasionally for years at a stretch — before returning to it . To help the reader through these abruptly changing interests , I have treated the successive phases of his life as though each were a career in a separate science , and the chapter headings reflect that choice . Readers after one specific facet of his life , rather than the whole of it , should therefore find the index guide enough . My own conviction , all the same , is that the individual pieces mean far less in isolation than the whole of his activity does when taken together , and on that account I would encourage readers to try to live through Wegener's life as he himself experienced it — interruptions, reversals of opinion, fresh starts and all . Câu (1)–(2): Wegener nhiều lần đổi hướng nghiên cứu; tác giả tổ chức sách để độc giả theo dõi các giai đoạn ấy. Câu (3): Người chỉ cần tìm một khía cạnh có thể dùng phần tra cứu. Câu (4): Dù vậy, tác giả cho rằng toàn bộ cuộc đời có ý nghĩa hơn từng phần riêng lẻ, nên khuyên độc giả theo dõi trọn cuộc đời Wegener .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. recommend that the book be read in its entirety (khuyên đọc toàn bộ cuốn sách ). Đối chiếu paraphrasing: recommend encourage readers be read in its entirety the whole of his activity + live through Wegener's life Đáp án A “ Mô tả điều đầu tiên khiến ông muốn viết về Wegener ”: Cụm “first drew me to Wegener” nằm ở đoạn 4. Đoạn đang hỏi nói về cách độc giả nên đọc cuốn sách. Đáp án B “ Giải thích vì sao Wegener chuyển giữa nhiều lĩnh vực ”: Câu (1) có nói ông nhiều lần tạm gác hướng nghiên cứu, nhưng câu (2) giải thích vì sao tác giả tổ chức sách như vậy, không giải thích nguyên nhân Wegener đổi hướng. Đáp án D “ Chỉ ra những phần cuộc đời Wegener mà tác giả thấy hấp dẫn nhất ”: Cụm “one specific facet” ở câu (3) nói về nhu cầu của một số độc giả. Câu (4) lại đề cao toàn bộ hoạt động của Wegener, không chọn một phần yêu thích.

questions.prompt: What is said about Wegener in the sixth paragraph?
options: He made careful written records of all his observations.
He had little interest in promoting himself or his ideas.
He preferred to debate his theories with fellow scientists.
He held membership of numerous scientific societies.
questions.correct: He had little interest in promoting himself or his ideas.

explanation.step1: What is said about Wegener in the sixth paragraph ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Đoạn văn thứ sáu nói gì về Wegener?
explanation.step2: Đếm các đoạn văn xuôi từ đoạn bắt đầu bằng “Alfred Wegener is remembered…”: đoạn thứ sáu tương ứng với Đoạn 7 trong bản đánh số ở đây. Ta bắt đầu đọc từ đoạn đó để tìm nhận xét về Wegener. Đoạn 7 — Alfred Wegener is remembered
explanation.step3: Đoạn 7: He rarely took part in scientific societies, a few exceptions aside, and made no attempt to win influence or promote his ideas through professional networking and intrigue ; his hours went instead on reading and writing in his study, or gathering observations out in the field .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. He had little interest in promoting himself or his ideas . (Ông không mấy quan tâm đến việc quảng bá bản thân hoặc ý tưởng của mình .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: little interest in made no attempt to promoting himself or his ideas win influence or promote his ideas Đáp án A “ Ông ghi chép cẩn thận mọi quan sát ”: Nếu thấy hoạt động đọc và viết (“reading and writing”), em có thể liên tưởng đến việc ghi chép Nhưng đoạn 7 còn nói ông không giữ sổ ghi chép hay nhật ký (“kept no notebook or diary”); không có căn cứ để nói ông ghi lại mọi quan sát. Đáp án C “ Ông thích tranh luận về các lý thuyết với đồng nghiệp ”: Sai vì câu bằng chứng nói ông không tìm cách quảng bá ý tưởng và dành thời gian đọc, viết; nó không nói ông thích tranh luận. Đáp án D “ Ông là thành viên của nhiều hội khoa học ”: Nhắc đến các hội khoa học (“scientific societies”) dễ khiến em chọn nhầm Nhưng bài nói ông hiếm khi tham gia (“rarely took part”), chứ không nói ông là thành viên của nhiều hội.

questions.prompt: What does Adamczyk say about some other famous scientists?
options: They can be more easily understood by their biographers than Wegener can.
Their theories proved more durable than Wegener's did.
Their published work reached a wider readership than Wegener's.
They felt greater certainty about their ideas than Wegener did.
questions.correct: They can be more easily understood by their biographers than Wegener can.

explanation.step1: What does Adamczyk say about some other famous scientists ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Adamczyk nói gì về một số nhà khoa học nổi tiếng khác? Cần tìm điểm được so sánh với Wegener, chứ chưa vội đoán đó là học thuyết hay công trình của họ.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt giúp định vị trực tiếp; ta đọc nhanh đến đoạn 8, nơi nêu tên các nhà khoa học khác (“Einstein, Darwin and Newton”) => đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn 8 — Einstein, Darwin and Newton
explanation.step3: Đoạn 7: Of the thousands upon thousands of letters he sent and received across a lifetime , barely a few hundred remain , for he kept no notebook or diary documenting his days . Đoạn 8: Einstein , Darwin and Newton , for instance , each handed down an enormous archive — notebooks by the hundred and correspondence running to tens of thousands of items; Michael Faraday, for his part, filled lengthy journals with his musings and guesswork to sit beside his laboratory notebooks . The fuller the record a researcher bequeaths , in short , the more reliably a biographer can reconstruct how that person's thinking first emerged and later changed . Câu (2): Câu (2), đoạn 7: tư liệu của Wegener còn lại rất ít . Câu (2): Câu (2), đoạn 8: các nhà khoa học khác để lại kho tư liệu lớn . Câu (3): Câu (3), đoạn 8: tư liệu càng đầy đủ => người viết tiểu sử càng dựng lại quá trình tư duy đáng tin cậy . So với Wegener, những nhà khoa học kia dễ được người viết tiểu sử tìm hiểu hơn .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: A. They can be more easily understood by their biographers than Wegener can. (Người viết tiểu sử có thể tìm hiểu họ dễ hơn so với Wegener.) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: more easily understood the more reliably a biographer can reconstruct Cơ sở so sánh: Wegener chỉ còn barely a few hundred remain những người khác có an enormous archive. Đáp án B “ Học thuyết của họ tồn tại lâu hơn học thuyết của Wegener ”: Đoạn 3 có ý gợi liên tưởng đến sự tiếp nối của học thuyết (“descends from Darwin's theory”) Nhưng bằng chứng ở đây so sánh tư liệu để lại, không so độ bền học thuyết. Đáp án C “ Công trình xuất bản của họ có nhiều độc giả hơn công trình của Wegener ”: khi thấy đoạn 7 nói Wegener chỉ có ít công trình xuất bản (“Only a handful of published works”). Nhưng kho tư liệu ở đoạn 8 không cho biết số lượng độc giả. Đáp án D “ Họ tin chắc vào ý tưởng của mình hơn Wegener ”: Cụm “musings and guesswork” ở đoạn 8 có thể khiến ta nghĩ đến mức độ chắc chắn Nhưng đoạn này nói về khả năng người viết tiểu sử dựng lại tư duy, không so sánh sự tự tin của các nhà khoa học.

questions.prompt: What is Adamczyk's main point in the final paragraph?
options: People ought to plan carefully in order to reach their goals.
Much of what happens in people's lives is beyond their control.
Having good intentions is not by itself enough to succeed.
People place great value on the freedom to make their own choices.
questions.correct: Much of what happens in people's lives is beyond their control.

explanation.step1: What is Adamczyk's main point in the final paragraph ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Ý chính Adamczyk muốn nêu trong đoạn cuối là gì? Ta cần tìm thông điệp chung, không chỉ một chi tiết về Wegener.
explanation.step2: Đề chỉ rõ đoạn cuối (“final paragraph”) => đọc từ nhận định mở đầu đoạn 9, nơi tác giả nêu quan điểm của mình (“my settled view”). Đoạn 9 — my settled view
explanation.step3: Đoạn 9: It is my settled view that hardly any of us — and Wegener is no exception — genuinely authors the life we lead . We make plans , we reflect , we act , often to all appearances freely ; yet for the most part life simply 'befalls us' , and only in hindsight do we shape that run of accidents into a tidy story of intentions carried through . What this book offers , then, is an account at once of the life and science Wegener meant and planned to have and of the life and science that in fact 'befell him' — and the two , as will quickly become apparent, do not always coincide . Câu (1)–(2): Tác giả nêu rằng con người khó thực sự làm chủ cuộc đời : dù lập kế hoạch, phần lớn sự việc vẫn cứ xảy đến . Câu (3): Trường hợp Wegener cho thấy cuộc đời dự tính và cuộc đời thực tế không luôn trùng nhau . Phần lớn những gì xảy ra trong đời nằm ngoài sự kiểm soát của con người.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. Much of what happens in people's lives is beyond their control . (Phần lớn những gì xảy ra trong đời nằm ngoài sự kiểm soát của con người .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Much of what happens in people's lives for the most part + life simply 'befalls us' beyond their control hardly any of us + genuinely authors the life we lead Đáp án A “ Mọi người nên lập kế hoạch cẩn thận để đạt mục tiêu ”: Nếu skim thấy việc lập kế hoạch (“We make plans”), ta dễ tưởng đây là lời khuyên Nhưng tác giả dùng nó để đối lập với những gì thực tế xảy đến, không khuyên lập kế hoạch. Đáp án C “ Chỉ có ý định tốt thì chưa đủ để thành công ”: Từ chỉ ý định (“intentions”) có thể gây nhầm, nhưng đoạn này không bàn về ý định tốt hay sự thành công. Đáp án D “ Mọi người rất coi trọng quyền tự do lựa chọn ”: Cụm gợi cảm giác hành động tự do (“to all appearances freely”) chỉ nói về vẻ bề ngoài; tác giả nhấn mạnh con người không hoàn toàn kiểm soát cuộc đời.

passages.title: Transport survey
content: 📌 Transport survey

Respondent: Sadie Jones
Year of birth: 1991
Home postcode: [ _____ ]

Travelling by bus
Journey date: [ _____ ]
Purpose of journey: shopping and an appointment with the [ _____ ]
Reason for using the bus: cost of [ _____ ] was excessive
Boarding point: [ _____ ] Street
Problems with the bus service:
today's bus was [ _____ ]too few buses in the [ _____ ]

Travelling by car
Main destination by car: the [ _____ ]

Travelling by bicycle
Avoids cycling in the city centre because of [ _____ ]
Has no bicycle because the flat lacks [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man conducting a transport survey with a woman named Sadie. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:49] MAN: Hello, could I ask you a few questions? We're carrying out a survey about transport.
[00:54] SADIE: Sure, no problem.
[00:56] MAN: Great. To begin with, what's your name?
[00:59] SADIE: Sadie Jones.
[01:01] MAN: Thank you. Could you also give me your year of birth? I don't need the full date.
[01:08] SADIE: Of course. I was born in 1991.
[01:11] MAN: And your postcode?
[01:17] MAN: Thanks. Is that part of Wells?
[01:20] SADIE: No, I live in Harburn, actually. Wells is quite close, though.
[01:25] MAN: I know the area well. My grandmother used to live there when I was young.
[01:29] SADIE: It's a lovely place.
[01:32] MAN: Now, thinking about the journey you made today, did you come by public transport?
[01:37] SADIE: Yes, I took the bus.
[01:39] MAN: Right. And today is the 24th of April, correct?
[01:44] SADIE: I thought it was the 25th. Oh, no, you're right. It's the 24th.
[01:50] MAN: Good. What brought you into town? I notice you've been shopping.
[01:55] SADIE: I bought a few things, yes. But I mainly came for an appointment with the dentist.
[02:01] MAN: Not the nicest reason for a trip. I hope there wasn't a problem.
[02:06] SADIE: Nothing serious. Just a routine checkup.
[02:09] MAN: Do you usually take the bus when you come into the city center?
[02:13] SADIE: I do. I gave up driving in because spaces are hard to find and the parking is so expensive.
[02:20] MAN: Right.
[02:21] SADIE: The bus is more convenient as well. And the journey is only around half an hour.
[02:26] MAN: That's fairly quick. Where did you board it today?
[02:29] SADIE: At the stop on Klaxby Street.
[02:31] MAN: Let me check the spelling. C-L-A-X-B-Y.
[02:35] SADIE: Yes, that's correct.
[02:40] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen carefully and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:22] MAN: Overall, are you happy with the service or is there anything you complain about?
[03:27] SADIE: It's quick and convenient when it keeps to the timetable, but today it was late. It was only 10 minutes, though it was still irritating.
[03:37] MAN: I can understand that. How do you find the timetable generally?

[03:41] SADIE: I mostly travel during the day, so it's usually fine. But whenever I've stayed in town in the evening, perhaps for a meal or a film, I've had to wait ages because buses are much less frequent.
[03:56] MAN: Thanks. I'd like to ask about traveling by car now.
[04:00] SADIE: I own one, but I hardly use it. I mainly drive to the supermarket. My husband takes it to the golf club at weekends, but that's really all.
[04:12] MAN: And do you cycle?
[04:13] SADIE: I don't have a bicycle at present.
[04:16] MAN: Have you ever used one of the higher bikes in the city?
[04:18] SADIE: No. I don't enjoy cycling in the center because of the pollution. I would like to buy a bike, though. It would be useful for commuting.
[04:29] MAN: What's stopping you from getting one?
[04:31] SADIE: I live in a second floor flat and there's no storage. We'd have to keep it in the corridor outside.
[04:39] MAN: Understood.
[04:43] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

questions.prompt:
Respondent: Sadie Jones
Year of birth: 1991
Home postcode: _____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.

passages.title: Becoming a volunteer for ACE
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Becoming a volunteer for ACE"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a representative from ACE explaining how people can become volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Good evening everyone.

[00:51] AUDIO: Welcome and thank you for coming along to learn about joining ACE as a volunteer. We support local residents and public services and we need some additional people to help us continue that work. Before I begin, I hope you're sitting comfortably. We added enough chairs so nobody would be left standing, although that has made things rather cramped for those at the back.

[01:18] AUDIO: The session should take only about 30 minutes, so I hope you'll manage. People often ask whether there is a particular age requirement, volunteers may be 16 or they may be over 60, suitability depends on the role. In practice, qualities such as being dependable matter far more and we have not found reliability to be connected with age. We're also asked what preparation is provided.

[01:51] AUDIO: There is a substantial amount and all of it happens in person. It continues throughout your involvement before you begin, while you're working and afterwards. Experienced volunteers normally deliver it since our managers are busy with other responsibilities. Before submitting an application, please think seriously about two things.

[02:19] AUDIO: We don't assess your motivation. People join for all sorts of reasons, from gaining experience to fulfilling a long held aim. What matters first is whether you genuinely have sufficient time for the role. If fitting it in would create pressure, volunteering may not be right for you.

[02:43] AUDIO: Your income isn't something we examine either. You decide whether unpaid work is practical. What we do expect is real commitment. Some volunteers have very modest incomes but still devote themselves completely to their responsibilities.

[03:06] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen carefully and answer questions 16 to 20. Let me now outline several areas where help is needed, along with the qualities that are particularly useful in each. One option is fundraising.

[04:03] AUDIO: We'd love volunteers who can suggest original and imaginative ways to bring in money, as simply holding a collection box outside shops or in the street can become monotonous. We also organize outdoor litter collection. You may need to walk for hours and sometimes climb slopes, so a good level of fitness is valuable. A number of regular participants are older, but they're energetic and care deeply about the environment.

[04:36] AUDIO: Anyone who likes working with youngsters might consider one of our three Playmate Vacancies. These volunteers use after-school activities to teach children about healthy living. Being a parent isn't necessary, but some understanding of food and diet, plus the ability to explain things clearly, is helpful. Alternatively, our Story Club for Children with Disabilities needs support, especially from people who've performed on stage.

[05:10] AUDIO: The Club Stages 3 shows each year, based on books the children have read, so help with the theatrical elements is always welcome. Finally, there is our First Aid Team. Members may eventually teach injury prevention to vulnerable groups. At the start, however, you'll need to absorb a large amount of information and remember every essential step and detail.
[05:40] AUDIO: Right? Does anyone have any questions?

Nhưng ngay sau đó có từ nối “although” báo hiệu một vấn đề trái ngược: “that has made things rather cramped for those at the back” . Cụm “rather c

options: Other personal qualities matter more than age.

questions.correct: Other personal qualities matter more than age.

explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "People often ask whether there is a particular age requirement, volunteers may be 16 or they may be over 60, suitability depends on the role. explanation.step3: ❓ Câu hỏi : What point does the presenter make about volunteers' age? ✅ Đáp án đúng : A. Other personal qualities matter more than age. ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Đoạn người nói đề cập trực tiếp đến yêu cầu về độ tuổi : “People often ask whether there is a particular age requirement …” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Đọc câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa cần nghe: volunteers' age và what point does the presenter make (= người nói muốn nhấn mạnh điều gì về độ tuổi tình nguyện viên ). Trong audio, người nói nói rằng tình nguyện viên có thể 16 tuổi hoặc trên 60 tuổi và sự phù hợp phụ thuộc vào vai trò → điều này cho thấy không có một độ tuổi cố định là quan trọng nhất. Sau đó, người nói nhấn mạnh: “qualities such as being dependable matter far more” → những phẩm chất

Tiếp theo là câu quan trọng nhất: “Being a parent isn't necessary, but some understanding of food and diet ... is helpful.” → Từ khóa food and diet tương ứng với knowledge of healthy eating . Trong audio, người nói nói rõ: “especially from people who've performed on stage” . Cụm “performed on stage” tương ứng trực tiếp với experience of performing . passages.title: Talk on jobs in fashion design
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Talk on jobs in fashion design"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two fashion students discussing a talk about careers in the industry. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:49] HUGO: Hi, Chantal. So, what did you make of the talk?
[00:53] CHANTAL: Hi, Hugo. I enjoyed it once I had changed seats.
[00:57] HUGO: Oh, were some students beside you talking?

[01:00] CHANTAL: No, that wasn't the problem. I arrived early so there were plenty of seats and I wouldn't have to stand. Then a very tall man sat directly in front of me and completely blocked my view.
[01:15] HUGO: Right. Seeing through someone's head isn't really possible, is it?
[01:19] CHANTAL: Exactly. Anyway, the session was very engaging, particularly the part about employment in fashion.
[01:27] HUGO: I thought so too. We already knew it was a fiercely competitive field, so none of us expects finding work to be easy.
[01:36] CHANTAL: True. And obviously not everyone will land their ideal position.
[01:40] HUGO: What surprised me was how many different kinds of work there are. Several we'd never considered, such as fashion journalism.
[01:48] CHANTAL: Same here. I had no idea the choice of careers was so broad.
[01:53] HUGO: The presenter delivered a fairly forceful message overall, didn't she?
[01:59] CHANTAL: She did. She kept implying that she understood our assumptions and then correcting us about the reality.
[02:07] HUGO: Maybe she believes students have a rather limited picture of the sector.
[02:11] CHANTAL: Even so, some of her comments about us seemed unnecessarily severe. We already know the industry is demanding.
[02:20] HUGO: Exactly. And we're only in our first year. Naturally, there's still a great deal for us to learn.
[02:27] CHANTAL: Do you think our secondary schools should have concentrated more on career preparation?
[02:33] HUGO: We were given plenty of careers talks at the right stage, which was useful, but the speakers weren't very motivating. Schools should invite more professionals like today's presenter.
[02:46] CHANTAL: I agree. The quantity and timing were fine. The weakness was that the advice didn't come from people with genuine first-hand expertise.
[02:57] HUGO: Has today's session changed your ideas about the career you might pursue?
[03:01] CHANTAL: I've decided to complete the course before choosing. I want to stay open to every possibility until the end.
[03:09] HUGO: I disagree. I think we should select one branch of fashion now and start developing specialist skills in it.
[03:18] CHANTAL: Then we'll have to disagree about when that decision should be made.
[03:22] HUGO: One thing seems certain. According to the presenter, we'll probably spend quite a while working as unpaid assistants.
[03:30] CHANTAL: Hmm.
[03:31] HUGO: I'm prepared to accept that as the reality of entering the industry, aren't you?
[03:37] CHANTAL: No, I'm not willing to accept it.
[03:39] HUGO: Really? The presenter knows the business and everyone else says the same thing.
[03:44] CHANTAL: That still doesn't mean it must happen that way for me.
[03:47] HUGO: Fair enough. I hope you prove them wrong.
[03:52] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:37] CHANTAL: The presenter's description of her first position was fascinating.
[04:41] HUGO: Yes. She was fortunate to become a musician's personal dresser without even applying. The opportunity simply appeared and she was paid to select all his clothes.
[04:53] CHANTAL: It must have been exciting, but she wasn't chasing fame or a large income. At that stage, experience was all she wanted.
[05:03] HUGO: And the musician criticised her for caring more about her own appearance than about his.
[05:09] CHANTAL: She admitted he was right. That made me reflect on how much attention I give my own clothes when the client's image should be the priority.
[05:19] HUGO: She clearly regretted losing that job.
[05:22] CHANTAL: Yes. She said she should have concealed how much she disliked the client instead of making those negative feelings obvious.
[05:31] HUGO: It was impressive that she recovered and accepted a retail job afterwards. Imagine going from dressing a musician to working in a shop.
[05:41] CHANTAL: She actually advised all future designers to try retail. I suppose you could learn things such as the sizes customers most often need.

[05:51] HUGO: She said figures about shopping time or seasonal buying aren't the main issue for designers, and average sizes are mainly a manufacturer's concern. What would help us is spotting a market gap. A design customers want but no shop currently offers.
[06:10] CHANTAL: Yes, customers continue looking when they can't find the right item. They also bring clothes back when something is wrong.
[06:18] HUGO: Exactly. Working in a high-end store could show you why products are returned. For example, if an expensive garment falls apart after being washed.
[06:30] CHANTAL: That sort of information would definitely be valuable.
[06:34] HUGO: Absolutely.
[06:38] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 Elephant translocation
Reasons for overpopulation at Majete National Park

Problems caused by elephant overpopulation

Advantages of translocation at Nkhotakota Wildlife Park

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a presentation about relocating groups. You will hear a presentation about relocating groups of elephants to a new reserve. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[00:53] AUDIO: In today's presentation, I'm going to explain how groups of elephants have been transferred to new reserves and established there. This process, called translocation, has taken place in Malawi in recent years because elephant numbers in some areas had grown too high. Overpopulation may sound like a welcome problem, and it is certainly unusual. Poachers had previously eliminated the elephants in Mahieti National Park for their ivory.

[01:23] AUDIO: However, the park was restocked in 2003, and strict law enforcement followed. No elephants have been poached there since, and the protected population bred so successfully that the park could no longer support all of them. This created several difficulties. Competition for the limited food supply increased, leaving some elephants hungry and forcing them to search farther away.

[01:56] AUDIO: They also regularly knocked down the fences around the park, and repairing them was expensive. The solution was to transfer dozens of elephants from Mahieti to Nakotakota Wildlife Park, which had none. Moving such large animals to a reserve 300 kilometers away was, of course, a considerable undertaking. So, what did the translocation involve in practical terms?

[02:30] AUDIO: The animals traveled in groups of eight to twenty, with every member drawn from the same family. Their social bonds meant the whole group had to move together. Vets and park rangers flew above them in helicopters, rounding up the selected elephants and directing them towards a designated open plane. The vets then immobilized the animals using tranquilizer darts.

[02:59] AUDIO: Choosing the correct dose for elephants of different sizes was difficult, especially while they were running. The team also had to finish this stage rapidly, so that the stress caused was kept to a minimum. Once the elephants started falling to the ground, staff immediately moved in. There was a danger of suffocation if an elephant landed on its chest, because that position could compress its lungs.

[03:31] AUDIO: Every animal therefore had to be rolled onto one of its sides. A member of the team stayed beside each elephant, while the vets carried out checks. Its breathing was monitored continuously. Fewer than six breaths a minute required urgent treatment.

[03:53] AUDIO: A tracking collar was placed on the matriarch of every group. The team recorded measurements of each animal's tusks, since large tusks increased the risk from poachers and also measured its feet. The elephants were moved to a recovery site, then loaded onto trucks for the journey to their new reserve. The animals settled successfully at Nkota Kota, and the project benefited local people as well.

[04:23] AUDIO: Employment opportunities rose substantially, improving living standards across the community. Former poachers could now obtain dependable incomes, and many voluntarily surrendered their weapons because they no longer needed them. More than 24 calves have been born since the relocation, and the park's 1,800 square kilometers provide ample room for further growth. The elephants are helping to restore the damaged ecosystem, while the project offers a sustainable conservation model for other parks.

[05:03] AUDIO: They have also attracted far more tourism, whose contribution to GDP is five times greater than that of the illegal wildlife trade. Interest has continued to rise dramatically. That is the end of part four.

passages.title: Working at Milo's Restaurants
content: 📌 Working at Milo's Restaurants
Benefits
[ _____ ] is arranged for all staff.A [ _____ ] is available on weekdays at every Milo's restaurant.A [ _____ ] is paid for when a shift finishes after midnight.
Person specification
Applicants must be able to cooperate effectively with a team.They must be committed to a high standard of [ _____ ].They must hold a qualification in [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man speaking. You will hear a man speaking to a recruitment advisor about jobs at a restaurant chain. First you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:49] WOMAN: Am I right that you're looking for work in a restaurant?
[00:52] MAN: Yes, I've worked in that sort of environment before and I can supply references.
[00:57] WOMAN: Good. We can go through those later. Milo's restaurants have several vacancies at present. They're regarded as a very good employer and offer quite a few benefits.
[01:11] MAN: That sounds promising.
[01:13] WOMAN: They have an excellent reputation for looking after their staff. For instance, every employee receives training, including people on temporary contracts.
[01:25] MAN: Really? You don't often find that, do you?
[01:28] WOMAN: No, you certainly don't.
[01:31] MAN: Are uniforms supplied free as well?

[01:34] WOMAN: Let me see. It just says staff must wear a white t-shirt with black trousers, so apparently not. However, because Milo's is a large chain, employees can use a discount at any of its restaurants during the week.
[01:50] MAN: Does that include Saturdays and Sundays?
[01:53] WOMAN: No, although you'll probably be working on those days anyway.
[01:58] MAN: True. Most branches are in the city centre, aren't they? So I could reach them easily by bus.
[02:05] WOMAN: Yes, that's right. And if you're on a late shift that ends after midnight, the company pays for a taxi to take you home.
[02:13] MAN: I doubt I'd need that. I'd probably cycle.

[02:17] WOMAN: All right. They also have some fairly precise requirements for applicants. Milo's is a young, energetic business and wants to build a strong team, so you need to fit in and work well with other people.
[02:31] MAN: That wouldn't be a problem. It actually appeals to me. My previous workplace was demanding, too, and we were expected to maintain a very high standard of service.
[02:43] WOMAN: That's useful because service is just as important at Milo's. They want staff who notice the small details.
[02:51] MAN: Fine. I'm accustomed to working like that.
[02:56] WOMAN: Excellent. The only other requirement is strong communication, so you'll need a qualification in English.
[03:03] MAN: That's fine.
[03:07] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:50] WOMAN: Now let's consider the vacancies Milo's currently has. The first is on Wivenhoe Street.
[03:55] MAN: Sorry. What was the street called?
[03:59] WOMAN: Wivenhoe. W-I-V-E-N-H-O-E. It's quite central, just off Cork Street.
[04:11] MAN: I see.
[04:12] WOMAN: The vacancy there is for a breakfast supervisor.
[04:15] MAN: I'd be happy with that.
[04:17] WOMAN: You'll probably know the sort of duties involved. You check, for example, that the portions are correct and make sure the procedures for keeping all the equipment clean are followed.
[04:30] MAN: Right. What does it pay? My previous job was £9.50 an hour and I was hoping for slightly more.
[04:40] WOMAN: The starting rate is £9.75 an hour. After three months, it rises to £11.25. That's reasonable.
[04:52] MAN: I assume the day begins very early.

[04:55] WOMAN: Yes, that's the main drawback. On the other hand, your afternoons and evenings would be free. Breakfast service starts at 7 and you'd arrive at 5.30 to prepare everything. You'd finish at 12.30. Well, having the rest of the day free would be useful.
[05:13] WOMAN: There's another role you may want to consider at the City Road branch. It's a junior chef position, so again there's some responsibility.
[05:23] MAN: Actually, I might prefer that one.
[05:26] WOMAN: You'd support the sous-chef and the other senior chefs. You'd also ensure there was sufficient stock each week and organise all the deliveries.
[05:36] MAN: I haven't handled that before, but it sounds manageable once I've learned the routine.
[05:41] WOMAN: Yes, and at first you'd work alongside experienced staff so it shouldn't cause any difficulty. The pay is a little better, £23,000 a year.
[05:54] MAN: Right.
[05:55] WOMAN: If your work is good, promotion can happen quite quickly, which is worth considering.
[06:02] MAN: It does sound interesting. What sort of hours would I work?

[06:06] WOMAN: The usual pattern, I think. There is plenty of evening and weekend work. Restaurants close on Mondays, but once every four weeks, you also get a Sunday off. Would you like me to send you...
[06:22] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check.

passages.title: The new housing development
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "The new housing development"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a communications manager speaking at a public meeting about a proposed housing development. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good evening, everyone.

[00:51] AUDIO: It's encouraging to see so many local people here for our presentation about the new housing development proposed for the edge of Nunnston. I'm Mark Reynolds, the developments communications manager. I'll begin with a short outline of the scheme, including why this particular piece of land was selected. It's currently used for agriculture, as is much of the area around Nunnston.

[01:21] AUDIO: However, the town's new industrial centre has created considerable demand for homes near people's jobs. At the moment, many employees have very long journeys to and from work, so building here would make life much easier for them. The international airport is only about 20 minutes away by car. That's useful, of course, but it wasn't a leading reason for our choice.

[01:50] AUDIO: Of greater importance was the excellent hospital 15 kilometres away, with a large secondary school even nearer. The steep slope is one disadvantage of the site, although the plans have been adapted to deal with it, so we don't expect it to cause serious difficulty. The plans have received a great deal of favourable feedback. People welcomed the range of housing types and prices, and they liked being within a short drive of the countryside.

[02:23] AUDIO: Although the development itself won't be in a rural setting, we were especially pleased by support for the layout. Most respondents felt it suited the natural landscape, and they approved of the efforts to preserve trees and wildlife. A number of people asked us to improve provision for cyclists, which we'll consider. Overall, though, residents thought the design and shared facilities would help people of different ages live together as a genuine community.

[02:58] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the presentation, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Now I'll show you a map of the proposed development. Its southern edge follows the main road, which continues towards Nunston, while London Road forms the boundary on the west.

[03:54] AUDIO: The site will contain roughly 400 houses and three apartment blocks. We're also providing a school for children aged 11 and under. Start at the south entrance at the bottom of the map, and follow the road running north through the site. The school will stand on that road, on the corner of the second, turning on the left.

[04:20] AUDIO: A large sports centre will offer both indoor and outdoor activities. It will be on the western side of the development, immediately below the road that branches away from London Road. Residents will have a clinic for medical problems. Find the lake near the top of the map.

[04:41] AUDIO: The clinic will be directly below it on the right-hand side of a row of houses. There'll be a community centre for every age group as well. In the northeast, you can see a row of specially designed homes for people over 65. The community centre will be directly beside those homes.

[05:04] AUDIO: Shopping has been included too. The supermarket will lie between the west and south entrances. The three mature trees close to London Road are being retained, and the supermarket will be immediately south of them. Younger children will have a playground.

[05:24] AUDIO: Follow the road north from the south entrance until it bends left at the top. The playground will occupy the inside of that bend and will look towards the lake. Right, before I take your questions, is there anything else you'd like me to explain about the plan? That is the end of part two.
[05:46] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students preparing a presentation about the lucky eruption. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:52] ADAM: Shall we get started on the presentation, Michelle? We haven't got much time left.
[00:57] MICHELLE: Yes, Adam. At least we finished all the background reading. I found it fascinating. I hadn't even heard of the lucky eruption before this.
[01:08] ADAM: Nor had I. Still, 1783 was a very long time ago.
[01:14] MICHELLE: It was, but the eruption was enormous and its consequences were devastating.

[01:20] ADAM: True. I liked having so many first-hand accounts to study. They really show how disastrous the volcano was, and how people were beginning to work out the science behind events like this.
[01:33] MICHELLE: Exactly. But for me, the more important point was the way it influenced political developments, both directly and indirectly, as well as having major social and economic effects.
[01:47] ADAM: I agree. That ought to be the central theme of our presentation.
[01:51] MICHELLE: The records made at the time were useful too, weren't they? The descriptions were remarkably consistent, even though the writers didn't always use identical terms.
[02:04] ADAM: Yes. What amazed me was how many weather observation stations already existed. Their records let us see changes in the weather, sometimes hour by hour.

[02:16] MICHELLE: Contemporary writers used the expression, Locky Haze, for the volcanic mist that moved across Europe. They knew it wasn't ordinary fog. This was before industrial pollution, so a fog that smelled of sulfur was completely unfamiliar.
[02:35] ADAM: Yes, that's a good point.
[02:37] MICHELLE: Accounts from the period connected the haze with more headaches, breathing difficulties, and asthma attacks. They also said it veiled the sun and turned it an unusual red color.
[02:49] ADAM: That must have looked extraordinary.
[02:52] MICHELLE: Benjamin Franklin wrote about the haze as well. Did you see that? He was serving as the American ambassador in Paris then.
[03:01] ADAM: I did. At first, nobody understood that the haze had come from the volcanic eruption in Iceland.
[03:08] MICHELLE: And Franklin was the first person to identify its cause.

[03:13] ADAM: He's often given credit for that, but it isn't quite right. A French naturalist reached the conclusion before him, I'll need to check the man's name. Several other naturalists then arrived at the same explanation independently.
[03:30] MICHELLE: I see. We should cover the eruption's immediate effects, of course, particularly the huge number of deaths in Iceland.

[03:39] ADAM: Yes. You'd expect severe loss of life there, and you might also expect the ash cloud to travel rapidly. What I didn't anticipate was how long the effects lasted, or that unusual weather was still being recorded two years later as far away as North America and North Africa.
[03:59] MICHELLE: I found the scale of that hard to believe, too. It must have been terrifying, and people were powerless even when they knew the ash cloud was heading towards them.
[04:12] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:56] MICHELLE: We should go through the terrible consequences in individual countries. The effects were surprisingly varied.
[05:03] ADAM: Let's begin with Iceland, where farming was hit extremely hard.
[05:09] MICHELLE: One of the most striking effects was on livestock grazing in the fields. The animals became ill after eating plants contaminated with fluorine from the volcanic fallout.
[05:22] ADAM: Awful. In Egypt, the abnormal weather brought a serious drought. The Nile failed to flood, so the crops were ruined.
[05:30] MICHELLE: And Egypt was so far from the volcano. Yet the famine there caused a greater loss of life than in any other country. More people died than during the plague.

[05:43] ADAM: Next, the death rate in the UK rose sharply, probably because of respiratory disease. One account suggests it was roughly twice the normal level, with an unusually large proportion of the victims under 25.
[05:58] MICHELLE: People may also be surprised by the weather in the USA. George Washington recorded in his diary that Virginia remained snowbound until March. This was before he became president.
[06:12] ADAM: Yes, and chunks of ice were floating down the Mississippi, something that had never been seen before.
[06:19] MICHELLE: It's remarkable. Anyway, what do you think we should— That is the end of part three.

passages.title: Pockets
content: 📌 Pockets
Reason for choosing the topic
Although [ _____ ] to use, pockets may receive little attention from both shoppers and designers.
Pockets in men’s clothing

The 18th century saw the growing popularity of [ _____ ].A [ _____ ] put pockets into the linings of garments.The pockets gave the wearer somewhere to keep small objects.Larger pockets could be made for men working in a particular [ _____ ].
Pockets in women’s clothing

Compared with men’s pockets, women’s were less [ _____ ].Women were particularly worried about pickpockets.Pairs of pockets were connected with [ _____ ].They were secured around women’s [ _____ ] beneath skirts and petticoats.An opening in the cloth let women reach items such as [ _____ ].Pockets of different sizes remained concealed inside clothing for many decades.Fitted dresses made hidden pockets harm a woman’s [ _____ ].‘Pouches’ became fashionable before the modern [ _____ ] appeared.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a student giving a presentation about the history of pockets in European clothing. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good morning.

[00:52] AUDIO: We were asked to select one feature of European clothing or fashion and explain how it has changed over time. I've chosen a fairly modest part of clothing—pockets. There are two main reasons for my choice. Almost everyone has pockets in things like jeans, jackets, and coats.

[01:12] AUDIO: We may carry bags or briefcases, too, but few things are as convenient as slipping a phone or credit card straight into a pocket. Despite being so useful, pockets receive surprisingly little thought and are often overlooked as an element of fashion. Looking back shows that pockets develop differently for men and women. Let's begin with men's fashion in the 18th century, when suits came into fashion.

[01:44] AUDIO: The trousers, known as breeches, stopped at the knee. Waste coats were short and jackets were long. All three garments had a cloth lining, and a tailor would sew pockets into it for the customer. Small objects, such as coins or pencils, could then be carried and reached through an opening in the lining.

[02:06] AUDIO: Men who wanted a stylish appearance increasingly had decorative pockets on the outside of their coats. However, a man in a profession requiring him to carry equipment, such as a doctor with medical instruments, might have larger, simpler pockets instead. Women's pockets followed a different pattern. To start with, they were far less visible than men's pockets and more difficult to reach.

[02:35] AUDIO: During the 18th and 19th centuries, women carried many possessions, some of considerable value, and wealthy women in particular were anxious about pickpockets. Their solution was to make two fabric pockets and join them with string. Poorer women might use recycled cloth, while those with more money could choose linen, perhaps with fine embroidery. The pair was fastened around the waist, so the pockets hung beneath the woman's clothes.

[03:08] AUDIO: Long skirts and several petticoats provided enough space to conceal many small belongings. An opening in the folds of the skirt allowed the wearer to reach an item, such as perfume. Working women also carried tools for their trade, but the pockets remained inside their clothing. They simply became larger or longer, sometimes extending as far as the knees.

[03:35] AUDIO: These tie-on pockets survived well into the 19th century. They began to disappear only when fashion changed near the end of the century, and dresses became slimmer and closer fitting. The hidden pairs then showed through the fabric and had an unwelcome effect on a woman's image. Women still needed somewhere to keep the personal items they were accustomed to carrying, so small bags known as pouches became fashionable.
[04:05] AUDIO: In time, these developed into the modern handbag, especially as pockets vanished from women's clothing altogether.

[00:51] BREDA: Hello, Wayside Camera Club, Breda speaking.
[00:55] DAN: Hi, my name's Dan and I'm calling because I'd like to become a member.
[01:00] BREDA: Wonderful, Dan. We have a membership form to fill in. We can do that over the phone and you can ask me anything you need to know as we go.
[01:10] DAN: Yes. That would be great. Thanks.

[01:18] DAN: Green. My full name is Dan Green.
[01:20] BREDA: And may I have your email address?
[01:23] DAN: Certainly. It's dan1068 at market.com.
[01:28] BREDA: Thank you. Now, where do you live?
[01:31] DAN: I'm in Peacetown, about ten miles from the club. I live in a house there.
[01:36] BREDA: Fine. What's the house number and the name of the street?
[01:41] DAN: It's number 52, Marrowfield Street.
[01:45] BREDA: Let me check the spelling m-a-double-r-o-w-f-i-e-l-d.
[01:53] DAN: Yes, that's correct.
[01:54] BREDA: And the town is Peacetown, right?
[01:56] DAN: That's right.
[01:58] BREDA: How did you find out about the club? Was it through the internet?
[02:02] DAN: That's normally where I'd look, but not this time. I was speaking to a relative recently and he recommended the club.
[02:11] BREDA: Is your relative one of our members?
[02:14] DAN: No, he's with a different club, but he'd heard very positive things about this one.
[02:19] BREDA: I see. What are you hoping to gain by joining us?
[02:23] DAN: I'm especially interested in your competitions. I really enjoy entering them.
[02:30] BREDA: Good. Is there another reason?
[02:32] DAN: Yes. I'd also like to socialise with other photographers.
[02:36] BREDA: Excellent. Which kind of membership are you interested in?
[02:41] DAN: What choices are available?
[02:44] BREDA: Full membership costs £30 per year, while associate membership is £20.
[02:50] DAN: In that case, I'll choose full membership.
[02:54] BREDA: That makes sense, since associate members aren't allowed to vote at meetings.
[03:03] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
[03:49] BREDA: I'd just like to learn a little more about your photography experience.
[03:54] DAN: Sure.
[03:54] BREDA: You mentioned competitions. Have you ever won one?
[03:59] DAN: Not so far, although I've entered three competitions before.
[04:04] BREDA: That's useful to know. Could you tell me about them, beginning with the first?
[04:09] DAN: The first competition was called Domestic Life.
[04:13] BREDA: So the subject had to be connected with the home?
[04:18] DAN: Exactly. I photographed a family having dinner together around a table. I didn't win, but the judges did give me some comments.
[04:30] BREDA: What feedback did they give you?
[04:32] DAN: They said the photograph looked too busy.
[04:35] BREDA: So their criticism was about the composition?
[04:39] DAN: Yes. Once they pointed it out, I understood where I'd gone wrong.
[04:44] BREDA: And what was the title of the second competition?
[04:47] DAN: My university was near the coast, where we often saw wonderful sunsets, and that became the competition theme.
[04:56] BREDA: Beautiful sunsets sound like an ideal subject.
[04:59] DAN: They were. But the rules said the shot had to include the clouds as well. A setting sun against a plain blue sky wasn't enough.
[05:12] BREDA: Of course, the clouds produced those striking pink and purple colours.
[05:18] DAN: Yes. I thought I'd captured them well, but the judges said I should have waited slightly longer before taking the photograph.
[05:28] BREDA: So the problem was the timing?
[05:31] DAN: Exactly. I took the picture too early. The third competition I entered was named Animal Magic.
[05:40] BREDA: That must have been a challenging subject.
[05:43] DAN: It was. I had to take hundreds of photographs.
[05:47] BREDA: I can imagine because animals rarely stay still.

[05:51] DAN: And movement was exactly what the photograph had to show. Eventually, I got a good picture of a fox. I took it at night though, and I suspected the image was rather dark. The judges agreed.
[06:05] BREDA: Well, Dan, you're clearly enthusiastic, and we'd be very happy to welcome you to the club. I'm sure we can help you improve in all the areas you've mentioned.
[06:16] DAN: Thank you. That sounds great.
[06:22] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Picking wild mushrooms
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Picking wild mushrooms"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a radio presenter introducing an author, introducing an author who gives advice about collecting wild mushrooms. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. We're very pleased to have Dan Beagle with us this evening.

[00:59] AUDIO: He has recently published a book about finding food that grows in the wild, and tonight he'll explain what people need to know before they go out collecting wild mushrooms. Thank you. I should begin with safety because it's essential to be certain about what you're doing. Several types of mushroom are highly poisonous.

[01:22] AUDIO: Once you learn to identify them properly, though, collecting them is well worth the effort. As there's an extraordinary range that you simply won't find in shops, even so, you must take care. I always advise people never to eat mushrooms gathered by friends or neighbors. Poisonous varieties can look remarkably similar to edible ones, so mistakes are easy to make.

[01:50] AUDIO: You should also stay away from mushrooms growing alongside roads with heavy traffic. As for flavor, freshly collected mushrooms are hard to beat. The ones sold in shops may already be a few days old and no longer at their best. There are also several common beliefs about wild mushrooms that need correcting.

[02:12] AUDIO: Some people claim that only pale or plain-looking ones are safe. But that isn't true at all. Certain edible varieties are bright red. I normally prefer mushrooms cooked, although eating suitable ones raw in a salad is harmless, and there's no need to peel them.

[02:33] AUDIO: Smell is not a reliable safety test, either. Some of the deadliest kinds apparently have almost no smell and may even taste pleasant. And if you see deer or squirrels eating a particular mushroom, don't assume it is safe for people. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

[03:32] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Mushroom collecting is usually linked with the countryside, but anyone without a car could begin in a nearby park. Parks often contain several suitable habitats, including open plain fields and wooded sections. The important thing is to arrive first thing in the morning because you'll face competition from wildlife as well as other collectors.

[04:04] AUDIO: In my local park, the deer often reach the best mushrooms before anyone else. If you're completely new to this, I wouldn't suggest going by yourself or depending on photographs in a guidebook, even mine. Some phone apps are excellent for identifying mushrooms, but in the middle of woodland, you may not get a reliable signal. The best approach, if you can arrange it, is to join a group led by an expert.

[04:33] AUDIO: That keeps you safe and helps you learn quickly. Conservation matters greatly, so there are a few simple rules to follow. Never clear every mushroom from one place. Take only what you actually need.

[04:46] AUDIO: Watch where you step so that you don't damage young mushrooms or nearby plants and leave any endangered species protected by law untouched. Several wild mushroom varieties have become less common in this region. Restaurants are showing more interest in locally sourced ingredients such as these, but the main cause is the large number of houses constructed here during the past decade. The development has increased demand for water from rivers and reservoirs while also destroying mushroom habitats.

[05:23] AUDIO: Let me add something about storage. Put the mushrooms into a brown paper bag while collecting them, then place them in the fridge as soon as you get home. They should remain usable for about two days, although cooking them sooner is preferable. Wash them thoroughly just before you cook them.

[05:45] AUDIO: Most people think they already know what mushrooms taste like, but wild varieties differ enormously. Be willing to experiment. They work well in all sorts of dishes, including stir-fries, risottos, and pasta. Remember, however, that some varieties can cause a bad reaction in certain people, so begin with a small quantity.
[06:10] AUDIO: Right, now I'm going to show you. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: Which TWO warnings does Dan give to people collecting wild mushrooms? (Answer 1 of 2)
options: Collect only one variety during each trip.
Avoid mushrooms growing near busy roads.
Never eat mushrooms gathered by somebody else.
Do not taste mushrooms until the collecting trip has finished.

passages.title: Automation and the future of work
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Automation and the future of work"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, you will hear two students, discussing a seminar about automation and the future of employment. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.

[00:53] YOUNG MAN: Yesterday's seminar about automation and where work is heading was excellent, wasn't it? Looking back at Britain's first industrial revolution in the 19th century and seeing how people responded to such enormous change really opened my eyes.

[01:10] YOUNG WOMAN: Same here. It was fascinating to learn what workers thought about mechanisation then and the problems it brought. I hadn't realised the earliest resistance came from textile workers.
[01:23] YOUNG MAN: Those protesters were the Luddites, weren't they? They smashed knitting machinery because they feared it would take away their livelihoods.
[01:32] YOUNG WOMAN: Yes, although in the end their campaign got nowhere. And overall, industrialisation produced more employment than it eliminated.
[01:42] YOUNG MAN: True, but none of that would have felt reassuring to them at the time. Their fear makes perfect sense to me.

[01:49] YOUNG WOMAN: Me too. Then the seminar turned to tomorrow's workplace and, unusually, the picture was very positive. I liked the suggestion that robots will handle dull, repeated tasks, leaving people with more worthwhile work. We normally hear nothing but gloomy forecasts.
[02:11] YOUNG MAN: I thought that part went too far. Take the claim that we'll have much more free time. How can that happen when the figures show we're working longer hours than ever?
[02:21] YOUNG WOMAN: I agree. And the prediction that fewer people will be unemployed didn't convince me either.
[02:28] YOUNG MAN: Maybe that could happen eventually, but I don't expect it any time soon.
[02:33] YOUNG WOMAN: No. And with people living longer, I think most of us will be required to stay in work until a later age.
[02:41] YOUNG MAN: We're already seeing that now.
[02:45] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:31] YOUNG WOMAN: The section on how technology has altered different occupations, and what might happen to them next, was especially interesting.

[03:40] YOUNG MAN: Absolutely. Accountancy was a surprise. You might assume new technology had removed many of those posts, yet the profession employs more people than at any earlier point. Accountants are still sought after, and their productivity has risen considerably.
[04:00] YOUNG WOMAN: Exactly. I couldn't believe there are 20 times as many accountants here as there were in the 19th century.
[04:08] YOUNG MAN: Nor could I. And demand for hairdressers has climbed dramatically over the past hundred years. Today there is one for every 287 people, rather than one for more than 1,500.
[04:22] YOUNG WOMAN: That's because people have more money left after essential expenses, so they can pay for personal services like haircuts more often.
[04:31] YOUNG MAN: Though the basic work itself hasn't been transformed much by technology.

[04:35] YOUNG WOMAN: No. Hair dryers have been introduced, of course, but hairdressing doesn't rely heavily on computers. Administrative work is a very different story. Technology has reshaped it completely.
[04:51] YOUNG WOMAN: As recently as 20 years ago, many secretaries spent their time taking dictation and typing.
[04:58] YOUNG MAN: Which sounds extremely repetitive compared with today, when administrative employees are trusted with broader duties and have a more respected role.

[05:09] YOUNG WOMAN: Yes, and it's now an area that attracts plenty of graduates. I was surprised the 19th century figure for farm workers wasn't higher. The 1871 census showed that about a quarter of the population worked in agriculture.

[05:25] YOUNG MAN: I'd have guessed over half. These days the proportion is below 0.2%. And care workers? There were hardly any in the 19th century because people generally didn't live as long. Now, however, demand for care services is certain to grow enormously.

[05:46] YOUNG WOMAN: We already struggle to provide enough of them. Bank clerks, by contrast, don't have a promising future. Their numbers have been shrinking since cash machines arrived in the 1980s.
[06:00] YOUNG MAN: And I think technology will make most of the work they currently do unnecessary.
[06:05] YOUNG WOMAN: I agree. Though things could still turn out differently, predicting the future is never easy.
[06:16] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Space Traffic Management
content: 📌 Space Traffic Management
A possible Space Traffic Management system

can be compared with Air Traffic Control, although it deals with satellites rather than aircraft.would introduce both legal and [ _____ ] measures to make operations safer.has not yet been established.
Challenges to creating an effective system

Satellites are now fairly [ _____ ], which has made them much more common.Some constellations may comprise [ _____ ] of satellites.Satellites do not currently have to send data that allows their [ _____ ].Only a limited number of methods are available for [ _____ ] satellites.Very small pieces of debris can be hard to detect.Operators may withhold details when satellites are used for [ _____ ] or commercial purposes.Establishing an object's exact [ _____ ] at a particular moment can be difficult.Scientists must rely on a [ _____ ] of the satellite's future path.
Possible solutions
Countries should agree on shared standards for presenting information.All the information needs to be held together in one [ _____ ].A coordinated system should inspire [ _____ ] among its users.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing the management of satellites and other objects orbiting the Earth. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. You will hear a lecturer discussing the management of satellites and other objects orbiting the Earth. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

[00:59] AUDIO: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In this astronomy lecture, I want to examine why we need a system that controls the movement of satellites and other objects travelling around the Earth. This is generally known as space traffic management. Air traffic control already operates internationally to help aircraft move safely through the skies.

[01:29] AUDIO: Space traffic management applies much the same idea to satellites. The purpose would be to reduce the risk of objects in orbit colliding with one another. Achieving that would require an agreed legal framework as well as technical systems capable of preventing these accidents. The difficulty is that no effective space traffic management system exists at the moment.

[01:58] AUDIO: So what has prevented one from being developed? To begin with, satellites are relatively cheap now compared with the past. So many more organisations can afford to send them into space. Instead of launching them individually, operators may deploy complete constellations containing thousands of satellites that work together.

[02:24] AUDIO: As a result, the space around Earth is becoming increasingly crowded. Yet after a satellite has been launched, there is currently no requirement for it to transmit information back to Earth that enables its identification. We have international arrangements that tell us where aircraft are and help keep them apart. But there are still far too few adequate systems for tracking satellites safely.

[02:54] AUDIO: Nor are complete satellites the only concern. The greater danger may come from the vast quantity of debris in orbit, including fragments of satellites and waste from space stations. Some pieces are so small that identifying them is extremely difficult, even though they can still cause serious damage. Another obstacle is that operators do not always want to release information about what they have launched.

[03:26] AUDIO: A satellite might serve military purposes, for instance, or have a commercial use, in which case its operator may not want rival organisations to know about it. Even when an operator is prepared to share data, obtaining it is challenging. We need details about the object and its location at a specific moment. A satellite is small and may be travelling at several thousand kilometres per hour, while no sensor can monitor such a fast-moving object continuously.

[04:03] AUDIO: Scientists, therefore, have to make a prediction about where it will travel next. Those are some of the principal difficulties. Turning to possible solutions, the treatment of information is especially important. We need a greater quantity of data, but it must also be available worldwide.

[04:24] AUDIO: That means agreeing on common standards for how the information is presented. Similar standards already exist in other scientific fields, so the task is demanding but achievable. As the information is gathered, it must then be brought together in a usable form. This would mean entering everything into a single database.

[04:52] AUDIO: Continued technological development will only make the space environment more congested. We therefore need a system that coordinates the activities of the many spacecraft operators. Just as importantly, it must establish trust among the people who use it, both within individual countries and internationally.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a telephone conversation between an employment agency advisor and a woman about an office vacancy. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:52] JULIE: Hello.
[00:53] GREG: Hi, am I speaking to Julie Davison?
[00:57] JULIE: Yes, that's me.
[00:59] GREG: It's Greg Preston calling from the employment agency. You came in last week to ask us about office-based positions.
[01:07] JULIE: Oh yes, I remember.
[01:09] GREG: We've just received information about a vacancy that I think could suit you.
[01:14] JULIE: Right.
[01:15] GREG: It's for a receptionist. If I remember correctly, you've worked in that kind of role before, haven't you?
[01:23] JULIE: I have. Before I got married and had my children, I spent two years working at a sports centre.
[01:31] GREG: Good. The post is in Fordham, so it isn't too far from where you live, and it's based at the town's medical centre.
[01:40] JULIE: Fine. Whereabouts is the centre?
[01:43] GREG: It's close to the railway station on Chasten's Road.
[01:46] JULIE: Could you repeat that?
[01:48] GREG: Chasten's Road. It's spelt C-H-A-S-T-O-N-S.
[01:56] JULIE: Got it, thanks. What sort of tasks would I have? Would I be answering patients' questions?
[02:03] GREG: Yes. You'd also arrange appointments, both at the desk and over the phone, and move them to another time when required.
[02:12] JULIE: That sounds straightforward enough.
[02:15] GREG: You'd also need to keep the centre's database current. There'd be some general office administration too, but those are the principal duties.
[02:25] JULIE: Okay.
[02:29] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:15] GREG: As soon as the information arrived, I thought of you. They say previous experience is essential, and you told us about the work you did at the sports centre.
[03:24] JULIE: Yes, I actually liked that position. Are there any other qualities they need?
[03:31] GREG: It's a very busy workplace, and patients may be anxious, so they need someone who stays calm under pressure while also being confident when dealing with members of the public.
[03:43] JULIE: Well, I've managed three children who are all younger than five, so I think I can handle that.
[03:50] GREG: I'm sure you can. They also specify that applicants need solid IT skills.
[03:57] JULIE: That's fine.
[03:58] GREG: Would you like to take the application further then?
[04:01] JULIE: Definitely. When is the person expected to begin?

[04:05] GREG: At the start of next month. But you should know the position isn't permanent. It's temporary, with the contract running only until the end of September. They have mentioned that other opportunities might come up afterwards.
[04:20] JULIE: Alright. What are the working hours?
[04:23] GREG: They need someone who can begin at 7.45 in the morning. Would that be possible for you?
[04:31] JULIE: Yes. My husband would get the children ready and take them to my mother's. She'll be caring for them while I'm working. And what time does the shift end?
[04:41] GREG: At 1.15. That would be fine.
[04:44] JULIE: I could collect the children on the way back and spend the rest of the day with them. By the way, can staff park at the centre?
[04:53] GREG: Yes. There's parking on the premises. And a bus also stops nearby.
[04:59] JULIE: Good. I'll probably drive, but that's useful to know. So what should I do next?
[05:06] GREG: If you'd like me to proceed, I'll send the centre your CV and references. After that, you should probably call them so they can set up an interview.
[05:17] JULIE: Excellent. Thanks very much.
[05:19] GREG: No problem. Goodbye.
[05:22] JULIE: Bye.
[05:25] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.
