passages.title: The Museum of Farming Life
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "The Museum of Farming Life"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a museum guide welcoming a group of visitors and giving some introductory information. First, you will hear a museum guide welcoming a group of visitors and giving some introductory information. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

[00:59] AUDIO: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Museum of Farming Life. As this is your first time here, I'll begin with a little background to the museum before describing some of the things you can explore today. The entrance where we're gathered belongs to a substantial building dating from 1880. It was first built as the private home of Alfred Palmer, a local businessman who owned the Palmer Biscuit Factory.

[01:30] AUDIO: The property was later sold, becoming student accommodation in 1911 and then a museum in 1951. A modern extension was added in 2005 to hold the collections. The university owns the museum. Two rooms are occupied by our museum offices, while the university uses most of the original building for classes.

[01:56] AUDIO: You'll probably notice students going in for lessons, although visitors aren't allowed inside that section. That's a pity, as it has some remarkable architectural details, particularly the room that was once the library. Fortunately, admission remains free, and that covers every gallery, the outdoor spaces, and the special exhibition rooms. Activities such as our museum club are free for children and students as well.

[02:27] AUDIO: There is a donation box nearby, but it's entirely up to you whether you put anything in and how much you give. There's a cloak room where coats and bags can be stored. Photography is permitted, unlike in many museums, so keep your cameras with you. Since the garden is rather chilly today, I'd also leave your coat on.

[02:50] AUDIO: However, carrying a heavy rucksack around isn't very comfortable, so I'd recommend putting large bags in the cloak room. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Now I'll take you through the different parts of the museum.

[03:50] AUDIO: The area called Four Seasons is positioned partly inside and partly beyond the main gallery. It shows a four-minute animated woodland scene, created especially for us by young people studying film. It's a lovely piece, and adults enjoy it just as much as children do. Our main gallery, Town and Country, contains photographs of award-winning sheep and the people who look after them.

[04:19] AUDIO: From there, you move into Farmhouse Kitchen, whose theme is fairly obvious. It houses the country's oldest collection of butter and cheese-making equipment. This morning, a specialist cheesemaker is demonstrating the process, and visitors may even be able to taste the results. Next, there are two possible directions.

[04:43] AUDIO: The staircase on the right leads to a landing overlooking the galleries. On the left is a year on the farm. We sometimes use that room for school visits, so it has plenty of seats and is a convenient place to rest. Anyone who wants a challenge can also try our memory quiz, answering questions about exhibits they've already seen.

[05:08] AUDIO: The following section is Wagon Walk, with farm carts collected from almost every region of the country. The differences between the areas are quite striking, and information panels beside the carts explain each one. Because these vehicles are old and delicate, adults must keep children close and make sure they don't climb on them. After Wagon Walk, you may return to reception, head into the garden, or revisit the galleries, so you aren't restricted to one route.

[05:44] AUDIO: Beezer Magic is in the garden's far corner. That section is currently being redeveloped, so it isn't open today, although honey from the museum is still available in the shop. The last place is the pond, home to several kinds of wildlife. There are ducklings only a few days old, as well as tiny frogs.
[06:08] AUDIO: The water is shallow and surrounded by a fence, making the area safe for children.

questions.prompt: What was the museum building first used as?

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The entrance where we're gathered belongs to a substantial building dating from 1880. It was first built as the private home of Alfred Palmer, a local businessman who owned the Palmer Biscuit Factory. The property was later sold, becoming student accommodation in 1911 and then a museum in 1951."
explanation.step3: ❓ Câu hỏi : What was the museum building first used as? ✅ Đáp án đúng : B. a private residence ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Đoạn guide bắt đầu nói về lịch sử tòa nhà: “The entrance where we're gathered belongs to a substantial building…” và ngay sau đó là câu “It was first built as the private home of Alfred Palmer …” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Đọc câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa cần nghe: first used as (= ban đầu được dùng làm gì ). Trong audio, guide nói rất rõ: “It was first built as the private home of Alfred Palmer” . Cụm private home tương đương với a private residence . Vì vậy, công dụng đầu tiên của tòa nhà là nhà ở tư nhân → chọn B . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ A. a commercial factory => Alfred Palmer là người sở hữu nhà máy bánh quy , nhưng tòa nhà này không phải

Two rooms are occupied by our museum offices, while the university uses most of the original building for classes.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Đọc câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa cần nghe: most of the original building now used for (= phần lớn tòa nhà gốc hiện được dùng để làm gì ). passages.title: Origami
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Origami"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two trainee teachers discussing a video of an origami lesson. First, you have some time. You will hear two trainee teachers discussing a video of an origami lesson. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 27.
[00:52] NARRATOR: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 27.
[01:00] TUTOR: I'd like you to talk about the lesson we've just watched and consider how origami might be used as an educational resource. Please discuss it with the person beside you.
[01:11] SEB: I'd never realized that something as basic as folding a square of paper into a shape, such as a bird, could be such an effective teaching tool. I see origami quite differently now.

[01:24] LIA: Same here. What interested me was the range of learning skills the children were developing. In the video, they listened very closely so that they could carry out every stage in the correct sequence and finish the bird.

[01:39] SEB: Exactly. They worked on their own in that lesson. But it would be useful to see whether they could figure out a simple model without any guidance. Doing that in groups could also encourage teamwork.
[01:53] LIA: Yes, though that would be considerably harder. What struck me most was that they were enjoying themselves at the same time as they were learning something unfamiliar.

[02:04] SEB: And that's especially important with children of that age. These pupils handled the folds easily, but with the younger class origami could be used to develop fine control of hand movements.
[02:16] LIA: Definitely. Shall we go through the individual children from the video? I noted all their names and made a few comments.
[02:25] SEB: Yes, I did as well.
[02:27] LIA: Great. Let's begin with Sid.
[02:29] SEB: He was worth watching because he'd been rather unsettled before the origami activity began.
[02:35] LIA: Yes. Having a practical task for his hands really helped him become calm and focus on what he was doing.
[02:43] SEB: I noticed that too. Then there was Jack. He seemed determined to solve each difficulty by himself.
[02:53] LIA: Yeah. He kept experimenting with different approaches instead of turning to the teacher. What did you think of Naomi?
[03:00] SEB: At one stage, she looked as though her attention was fading. But then she decided her mouse ought to be better than everyone else's. And that made her put in more effort.
[03:11] LIA: Even so, she didn't appear pleased with the finished model.
[03:14] SEB: No, she didn't.
[03:16] LIA: Anya was excellent. She followed the demonstration closely and made an ideal bird with hardly any difficulty.
[03:25] SEB: Yes. The teacher could probably have given her a more demanding version.
[03:31] LIA: Perhaps. I got the impression Zara had never tried origami before.
[03:36] SEB: She looked as if she couldn't understand what was happening.
[03:40] LIA: She was clearly uncertain about what she needed to do, although her final model was reasonably successful.
[03:47] SEB: Yes. I'm sure she still learned something useful from it.
[03:52] LIA: Yeah.
[03:55] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30.
[04:41] LIA: I think the activity succeeded partly because the teacher had prepared everything so thoroughly.

[04:47] SEB: Yes. It must have taken a long time to make a separate example for every stage of folding the bird, but it was worthwhile. The children could see the goal at each point, and being able to pick up the models was much more helpful than simply viewing diagrams.
[05:05] LIA: Those real models complemented her spoken directions very effectively.
[05:10] SEB: It's surprising that more teachers don't use origami. What do you think puts them off?
[05:18] LIA: They may assume it won't attract children who are accustomed to digital activities, particularly boys, even when they recognize its educational value.
[05:28] SEB: I'm not convinced. It's much like any other craft. My guess is that plenty of teachers simply aren't very skillful with their hands, like me.
[05:38] LIA: That's probably it. If practical work doesn't come naturally, preparing the activity can seem like too much effort.

[05:47] SEB: Anyway, we should use it during our year 3 maths placement. In the video, origami reinforced what the children already knew about geometric shapes. But it could also be a lively way to introduce fractions, which they'll study shortly.
[06:04] LIA: Good plan. Quite a few pupils in that class may find fractions difficult. Origami would help with symmetry too, although I think they covered that last term.
[06:14] SEB: Right. Let's collect some ideas and plan the lesson next week.
[06:18] TUTOR: All right. Could everyone stop there, please?

passages.title: Victor Hugo
content: 📌 Victor Hugo
Les Misérables
The novel has been adapted for both the stage and the cinema.People generally know more about its [ _____ ] than they do about Hugo himself.
Hugo’s early career

He became a successful writer in Paris and led the Romantic movement.He spoke publicly about social concerns such as [ _____ ] and education.His criticism angered Napoleon III, who sent him into exile.
Exile and Guernsey
During his exile, he lived in several places in [ _____ ].Earnings from a published collection of [ _____ ] enabled him to buy a house on Guernsey.
Hugo’s house

On the ground floor, valued objects include portraits, [ _____ ] and tapestries.He converted inexpensive wooden [ _____ ] into detailed wall carvings.Chinese influence can be seen in the first-floor wallpaper and [ _____ ].His library still holds many of his favourite books.His writing room at the top of the house looked across the [ _____ ].As well as writers, disadvantaged local [ _____ ] were invited to meals there.In 1927, Hugo’s [ _____ ] gave the house to the city of Paris.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a student giving a talk about the French writer Victor Hugo and his home on Guernsey. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. The writer I'm focusing on today is Victor Hugo.

[00:54] AUDIO: He is widely known because Les Miserables, published in 1862, has reached audiences far beyond France. It became a successful stage musical in the 1980s and was later made into a major film. As a result, many people can describe the novel's plot, at least in broad terms, while knowing surprisingly little about the man who created it. I'd like to fill in some of that background, particularly by looking at Hugo's house on Guernsey, one of the British Channel Islands.

[01:32] AUDIO: Before turning to the house though, it's useful to consider his public life. In Paris, Hugo was at the peak of a highly successful career and was regarded as the leading figure in the Romantic movement. His interests extended well beyond literature. He frequently addressed social problems in public speeches, including poverty, and he also argued that education needed reform.

[02:03] AUDIO: These opinions made him an influential social critic as well as a celebrated author. Napoleon III and the French authorities strongly objected to Hugo's open criticism. The Emperor eventually ordered him to leave Paris so Hugo was forced into exile. He lived in different parts of Europe before arriving on Guernsey in 1855, which was the third place where he settled outside France.

[02:35] AUDIO: Hugo was extremely productive during this period and completed major work while on the island. He bought a large house in St Peterport with money earned from publishing a collection of his poetry. It was the only property he ever owned and it clearly mattered a great deal to him. The house had five stories and Hugo lived there for 15 years.

[03:05] AUDIO: He returned to France in 1870 after Napoleon's empire collapsed. During his time on Guernsey, he personally shaped the appearance of every floor so imaginatively that the interior is often described as a work of art. The building is now a museum visited by large numbers of people. The ground floor preserves several things that Hugo valued.

[03:33] AUDIO: Portraits of family members hang there together with drawings he made while travelling and large tapestries that he helped design. The dark wooden wall panels are especially unusual. Instead of buying expensive material, Hugo found inexpensive wooden furniture at the market, took it apart and transformed it into elaborate carvings. Upstairs, two lounges were used for entertaining guests.

[04:03] AUDIO: One is decorated mainly in red and the other in blue. Both show a strong Chinese influence, particularly in the patterned wallpaper and the lamps. Hugo made the lamps himself after studying original Chinese examples. A library containing many of Hugo's favourite books forms the passage towards the third floor.

[04:29] AUDIO: At the top of the house is a bright room known as the lookout. Unlike the shadowy rooms below, it is enclosed by glass and overlooks the harbour. Hugo used this as his writing room and often worked there until lunchtime. The house also reflects Hugo's values.

[04:49] AUDIO: He welcomed other well-known writers but his hospitality was not limited to famous visitors. Once a week he invited a large group of local children from poor parts of the island to dinner and personally served their meal, which was a remarkable act for that period. Hugo's family retained the property after his death. In 1927, his relatives donated it to the city of Paris.
[05:21] AUDIO: The house has since been restored with the help of historical photographs and is now open to the public as a museum.
